The Scottish Borders: Britain's Best-Kept Riding Secret

While most motorcyclists head straight for the Highlands, the Scottish Borders offers some of the finest riding in Britain. Rolling hills, empty roads, and a landscape that shifts between pastoral valleys and wild moorland — all without the tourist crowds that plague more famous regions. It's the thinking rider's Scotland.

The A7: Edinburgh to Carlisle

The A7 is the Borders' spine — a flowing road that follows the valleys of the Gala Water and Teviot through the heart of the region. It's fast, well-surfaced, and rarely busy. The section between Selkirk and Langholm is particularly fine, with sweeping bends through rolling farmland.

The A708: Moffat to Selkirk

The A708 is arguably the Borders' finest road. From Moffat, it climbs past the Grey Mare's Tail waterfall (a 60-metre cascade visible from the road) to St Mary's Loch, then continues through wild, empty country to Selkirk. The road surface is excellent and the scenery alternates between dramatic and tranquil.

Devil's Beeftub (A701)

The A701 from Moffat to Edinburgh passes the famous Devil's Beeftub — a deep, natural amphitheatre where cattle rustlers once hid stolen livestock. The road climbs steeply out of Moffat with tight bends and emerges onto an open moorland plateau. It's dramatic and atmospheric, especially in low cloud.

The Scottish Borders has the best road surface-to-traffic ratio in Britain. You can ride for an hour without seeing another vehicle on some of these roads.

Classic Borders Loop

A perfect day ride: Melrose → Lauder → Heriot → Innerleithen → Traquair → Yarrow → Selkirk → Melrose. This 80-mile loop covers rolling hills, forest roads, and valley rides. Stop at Traquair House — Scotland's oldest inhabited house with its own brewery. Melrose has excellent pubs and the atmospheric ruins of Melrose Abbey.

More Borders Roads

  • B709 Eskdalemuir — Remote road through Craik Forest past the Samye Ling Buddhist monastery
  • A699/A698 Tweed Valley — Following the River Tweed through Kelso and Coldstream
  • B6357 Newcastleton Road — Wild road through Liddesdale on the English border
  • A72 Peebles to Biggar — Gentle valley road with views of the Pentland Hills

Practical Tips

The Borders has good fuel availability in the main towns — Melrose, Hawick, Selkirk, Peebles, and Jedburgh all have filling stations. Accommodation ranges from historic country houses to simple B&Bs. The region is accessible from Edinburgh (1 hour) and Newcastle (90 minutes), making it perfect for long weekends. Road surfaces are generally excellent — this is one of the best-maintained road networks in Scotland. keyTakeaways: The Borders offer some of Britain's emptiest, best-surfaced roads without the Highland tourist crowds.
The A7 is the region's spine, flowing through the Gala Water and Teviot valleys from Edinburgh to Carlisle.
The A708 from Moffat to Selkirk passes the 60-metre Grey Mare's Tail waterfall and St Mary's Loch.
The A701 climbs past the Devil's Beeftub, a dramatic natural amphitheatre once used by cattle rustlers.
Fuel is available in Melrose, Hawick, Selkirk, Peebles and Jedburgh; the region is an hour from Edinburgh.

faq.q: Why ride the Scottish Borders over the Highlands?
faq.a: The Borders has the best road surface-to-traffic ratio in Britain. You can ride for an hour without seeing another vehicle on some roads, all without the tourist crowds that plague more famous regions. Rolling hills shift between pastoral valleys and wild moorland, making it the thinking rider's Scotland.

faq.q: What is the finest road in the Borders?
faq.a: Many rate the A708 from Moffat to Selkirk as the region's finest. It climbs past the Grey Mare's Tail, a 60-metre cascade visible from the road, to St Mary's Loch, then continues through wild, empty country. The surface is excellent and the scenery alternates between dramatic and tranquil.

faq.q: Where can I fuel up in the Borders?
faq.a: Melrose, Hawick, Selkirk, Peebles and Jedburgh all have filling stations, giving good coverage across the region. Road surfaces are generally excellent, among the best-maintained in Scotland, so the Borders make an ideal long-weekend destination with reliable fuel and plentiful accommodation.

Very accessible. The Borders sit about an hour from Edinburgh and 90 minutes from Newcastle, making them perfect for long weekends. A classic 80-mile loop runs Melrose, Lauder, Heriot, Innerleithen, Traquair, Yarrow and Selkirk, with Traquair House and Melrose Abbey worth a stop.
